# **Decomposing Illumination and Intrinsic Surface Properties in 3D Gaussian Splatting for Scene Relighting**

## **Fundamental Principles of Gaussian Splatting Disentanglement**

Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models continuous 3D scenes by optimizing an explicit collection of volumetric Gaussian primitives characterized by mean positions ![][image1], spatial covariance matrices ![][image2]—decomposed into scale vectors ![][image3] and rotation quaternions ![][image4]—opacities ![][image5], and view-dependent colors parameterized via Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients1. Although 3DGS delivers real-time rendering speed alongside high photometric accuracy for novel view synthesis, its underlying formulation entangles geometry, surface material reflectance, and ambient lighting into the view-dependent SH parameters3. Consequently, placing a natively reconstructed 3DGS scene under a novel lighting environment yields severe visual conflicts, as baked-in specular highlights, ambient shadows, and color temperatures collide with the new illumination sources3.  
To decouple illumination from 3D Gaussian representations, software architectures must perform inverse rendering—a process that factorizes the radiometrical appearance of a scene into explicit physical attributes3. Mathematically, the outgoing radiance ![][image6] at a surface position ![][image7] along view direction ![][image8] is governed by the rendering equation:  
![][image9]  
where ![][image10] represents emitted radiance, ![][image11] denotes the unit upper hemisphere centered at surface normal ![][image12], ![][image13] is the incoming radiance from direction ![][image14], and ![][image15] is the Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF)4.  
In standard 3DGS, the spherical integral is implicitly fitted by the SH basis functions assigned to each primitive2. Achieving controllable relighting requires replacing these SH representations with an explicit factorization framework comprising four interdependent physical components:

> 1. **Surface Geometry and Orientations (![][image12])**: Extracting accurate surface normals for every primitive or rendered pixel to calculate the directional cosine falloff ![][image16]4.  
> 2. **Spatially-Varying BRDF (SVBRDF)**: Disentangling intrinsic material parameters, specifically diffuse base color (albedo) ![][image17], metallicness ![][image18], and surface roughness ![][image19]4.  
> 3. **Environment Illumination (![][image20])**: Parameterizing global incident light using high-dynamic-range (HDR) environment maps or localized light sources4.  
> 4. **Light Transport and Visibility (![][image21])**: Accounting for secondary optical effects, such as self-shadowing and diffuse interreflections, which standard forward point rasterization cannot natively trace4.

Inverse rendering from multi-view images is fundamentally an ill-posed under-constrained optimization problem, as infinitely many combinations of surface normals, albedos, and light configurations can synthesize identical pixel colors3. Resolving these ambiguities requires regularized geometric constraints, physically-based rendering (PBR) shading formulations, and structured multi-stage optimization workflows3.

## **Geometric Foundations and Normal Estimation Mechanics**

Accurate normal vector estimation serves as the geometric anchor for material and lighting separation. The orientation of a surface normal dictates the microfacet shading alignment, controlling both specular highlight position and diffuse light falloff3. Standard 3D Gaussians are volumetric ellipsoids optimized purely for spatial image rendering; as a result, they do not inherently possess well-defined surface boundaries or normal vectors2. To derive clean geometry from point-based primitives, current software frameworks follow two primary paradigms: normal regularization over 3D Gaussians or transition to oriented 2D Gaussian Surfels2.  
In the 3D Gaussian regularized paradigm, individual primitives retain a 3D covariance matrix ![][image22], where ![][image23] is a rotation matrix derived from a unit quaternion and ![][image24] defines principal axis scales2. To force volumetric ellipsoids to align with physical object boundaries, optimization frameworks flatten one scale dimension (![][image25]), allowing the shortest principal axis—represented by the third column of the rotation matrix ![][image23]—to serve as the primitive normal ![][image26]7.  
Because standard volumetric alpha blending aggregates primitives across depth channels, it frequently creates semi-transparent floating artifacts2. To counter this, frameworks such as GS-IR employ depth-derivation regularization4. Depth maps ![][image27] rendered via linear interpolation are differentiated across screen coordinates to compute pseudo-ground-truth geometric surface normals ![][image28]4. The explicit primitive normals ![][image29] are then aligned with ![][image30] via a cosine loss function4:  
![][image31]  
Self-regularization paradigms, such as GIR, refine normal fields by enforcing ray-facing visibility constraints14. A surface Gaussian contributes to color evaluation only if its shortest principal axis forms an obtuse angle relative to the camera viewing vector (![][image32])14. Gaussians violating this condition are filtered during the rendering pass, preventing opposing surface normals from blending into visible pixels14.  
In the 2D Gaussian Surfels paradigm, the 3D volumetric representation is replaced with 2D oriented planar disks embedded in 3D space2. Each 2D Gaussian surfel is defined by a 3D position ![][image33], two orthogonal tangent vectors ![][image34] and ![][image35] scaled by ![][image36], and an exact intrinsic surface normal ![][image37]2. 2DGS evaluates ray-splat intersections analytically rather than relying on local affine screen projections2. Geometry consistency across views is enforced using depth distortion and normal alignment losses2:  
![][image38]  
where ![][image39] represents the alpha-blended weighting at intersection depth ![][image40]2. By penalizing depth dispersion along individual camera rays, 2DGS collapses primitives into a tightly defined geometric shell, yielding consistent surface normals suitable for physically-based lighting evaluation10.

## **Physically-Based Rendering (PBR) & Material Factorization Architecture**

Once reliable geometric surface normals are established, the view-dependent Spherical Harmonics color attributes are replaced with physically-based material parameters4. Inverse rendering frameworks adopt microfacet BRDF models, most notably the Cook-Torrance formulation4. Under Cook-Torrance parameterization, surface reflection is split into a Lambertian diffuse component and a microfacet specular component4:  
![][image41]  
where ![][image42] denotes the half-way vector between light direction ![][image14] and view direction ![][image8]4. The intrinsic material parameters allocated per primitive or rendered pixel include:

* **Diffuse Albedo (![][image43])**: The base color of the surface free from lighting, highlights, or cast shadows4.  
* **Metallicness (![][image44])**: A scalar indicating whether the surface exhibits dielectric behavior (![][image45]) or metallic behavior (![][image46])4.  
* **Roughness (![][image47])**: A scalar defining microfacet orientation dispersion, governing specular highlight spread4.

The specular terms are calculated using standard microfacet functions4. The GGX/Trowbridge-Reitz normal distribution function ![][image48] determines microfacet alignment density4:  
![][image49]  
The Fresnel reflection factor ![][image50] is computed via the Schlick approximation using base reflectivity ![][image51]4:  
![][image52]  
The geometric shadowing factor ![][image53] evaluates self-masking across surface microfacets using Smith's joint formulation4.  
Software architectures store material parameters using either direct primitive storage or deferred neural feature representations3. In direct primitive storage, each Gaussian holds vector attributes ![][image54] alongside its spatial parameters4. Tile-based rasterization projects these attributes into screen-space G-Buffers (Albedo, Normal, Roughness, Metallic, Depth), after which image-space compute shaders evaluate the PBR rendering equation per pixel4. In deferred neural representations, Gaussians store spatial feature vectors ![][image55] that are decoded into material parameters by lightweight Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs)3. The implicit network acts as a spatial regularizer, suppressing high-frequency noise and prevent floating artifacts in raw albedo maps3.  
To avoid overfitting where strong specular highlights are improperly baked into diffuse albedo maps, advanced architectures incorporate decoupled appearance modeling3. The RTR-GS framework integrates an auxiliary reflection map branch to isolate high-frequency specularities from low-frequency radiance transfer components during optimization3. Similarly, the GS-ID framework leverages generative diffusion priors alongside deshadowing modules to guide material decomposition, ensuring that albedo outputs remain clean under drastic relighting changes5.

## **Light Transport, Visibility, and Occlusion Modeling**

Standard point-based Gaussian rasterization projects 3D primitives directly onto a 2D image plane in camera depth order2. Because ray paths between scene points and light sources are not traced during forward rasterization, standard 3DGS cannot model visibility ![][image56] or indirect interreflections ![][image57]4. If lighting separation is attempted without explicit transport modeling, the optimization solver compensates by darkening the albedo map to recreate missing shadows3.  
Direct environmental lighting is parameterized either via high-resolution 2D HDR equirectangular maps ![][image58] or spatially continuous Spherical Gaussian (SG) mixtures4. To model complex secondary illumination, frameworks employ volumetric caching, on-the-fly ray tracing, or parametric light encodings4.

\+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+  
|                                    LIGHT TRANSPORT ARCHITECTURES                                        |  
\+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+---------------------------------+  
| Volumetric Caching (GS-IR)        | On-the-Fly Ray Tracing (IRGS++)   | Parametric Encodings (GIR/GS-ID)|  
\+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+---------------------------------+  
| Voxels evaluate depth cubemaps    | OptiX BVH accelerates secondary   | View-direction SH coefficients  |  
| to cache ambient occlusion &      | rays to calculate exact shadow    | or adaptive Spherical Gaussian  |  
| indirect light as low-degree      | transmittance and multi-bounce    | Mixtures model local spatial    |  
| Spherical Harmonics grids.        | interreflections directly.        | light interaction.              |  
\+-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+---------------------------------+

In the volumetric caching approach (e.g., GS-IR), spatial grids are established across the scene bounding box to bake visibility and indirect light into voxel caches4. Occlusion volumes ![][image59] evaluate six depth cubemap faces ![][image60] from voxel centers4. Thresholding transforms these depth maps into binary visibility cubemaps ![][image61], which are integrated into low-degree Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients ![][image62]4:  
![][image63]  
Parallel indirect illumination volumes ![][image64] cache incoming radiance cubemaps as low-frequency SH coefficients4. During image synthesis, screen-space shading points query ![][image59] and ![][image64] via trilinear interpolation to evaluate ambient occlusion and diffuse indirect shading efficiently4.  
In the on-the-fly ray tracing approach (e.g., IRGS++), 2D surfels are structured into GPU-accelerated Bounding Volume Hierarchies (BVH) using OptiX10. For a shading point ![][image7] and light direction ![][image14], secondary rays ![][image65] are cast through the BVH15. Visiblity ![][image56] is computed by accumulating surfel opacities along the ray path15:  
![][image66]  
This ray-tracing core evaluates dynamic soft shadows and multi-bounce indirect light transport accurately, though it increases computational demand during training10.  
In parametric light encoding approaches (e.g., GIR and GS-ID), light transport is modeled using directional functions5. GIR parameterizes view directions within SH basis functions to approximate indirect interreflections14. GS-ID employs spatially distributed Spherical Gaussian Mixtures (SGMs), where each mixture unit models localized directional intensity ![][image67]5. Low-energy SGM units are iteratively pruned during training, leaving a compact representation of localized light sources5.

## **End-to-End Program Implementation Workflow**

To build a standalone program that extracts intrinsic materials from 3D Gaussian Splats and executes novel relighting, the software pipeline must execute four sequential processing stages. Attempting to optimize geometry, BRDF parameters, and lighting simultaneously from uninitialized states causes severe optimization divergence and unphysical solutions3.

\+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+  
|                                    END-TO-END FACTORIZATION PIPELINE                                    |  
\+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+  
| Stage 1: Geometry Warm-up & Normal Regularization                                                       |  
| \- Process multi-view RGB images and sparse COLMAP point clouds.                                         |  
| \- Optimize Gaussian spatial parameters under photometric, depth distortion, and normal alignment losses.|  
| \- Freeze spatial parameters (\\mu, S, q, \\alpha) upon geometric convergence.                             |  
\+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+  
                                                     |  
                                                     v  
\+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+  
| Stage 2: Light Transport & Visibility Precomputation                                                    |  
| \- Option A (Voxel Baking): Voxelize scene domain; render cubemaps; bake V\_{occl} and V\_{illu} SH grids.|  
| \- Option B (Ray Tracing): Construct GPU OptiX BVH tree over frozen 2D surfels.                          |  
\+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+  
                                                     |  
                                                     v  
\+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+  
| Stage 3: Joint BRDF & Lighting Factorization                                                            |  
| \- Allocate learnable materials (a, m, \\rho) to Gaussians and initialize target HDR environment map.    |  
| \- Rasterize G-Buffers; compute image-space Cook-Torrance PBR shading with visibility corrections.       |  
| \- Minimize combined photometric, total variation albedo smoothness, and metallic bimodal losses.      |  
\+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+  
                                                     |  
                                                     v  
\+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+  
| Stage 4: Interactive Relighting Engine                                                                  |  
| \- Replace original environment map with custom target HDR maps or directional light sources.            |  
| \- Execute image-space deferred PBR rendering using rasterized intrinsic G-Buffers.                      |  
\+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

### **Stage 1: Geometry Initialization and Normal Alignment**

The software program ingests posed multi-view RGB images alongside a sparse COLMAP point cloud1. 3D or 2D Gaussians are initialized at point locations1. The system trains primitive spatial positions, scales, rotations, and opacities for ![][image68] to ![][image69] iterations using photometric image losses (![][image70] and SSIM)5.  
Depth distortion loss ![][image71] and normal consistency loss ![][image72] are activated to force primitives into a smooth surface shell4. Adaptive density control routines split oversized primitives and prune transparent floaters2. Once normal fields stabilize (typically around ![][image73] iterations), spatial parameters (![][image74]) are frozen to prevent geometric drift during material optimization4.

### **Stage 2: Light Transport Precomputation**

With primitive positions fixed, the program constructs its transport visibility structure:

* **Voxel Baking Path**: The system instantiates a 3D spatial grid across the bounding box4. Depth and radiance cubemaps (![][image75] resolution per face) are rendered from voxel centers to calculate SH coefficients for occlusion volumes ![][image59] and indirect light volumes ![][image64]4.  
* **Ray Tracing Path**: The system populates an OptiX BVH acceleration structure with frozen 2D surfel primitives, configuring fast GPU ray-triangle or ray-dissect intersection kernels15.

### **Stage 3: Joint BRDF and Illumination Factorization**

Learnable material parameters are bound to each Gaussian: diffuse albedo ![][image76], metallicness ![][image77], and roughness ![][image78]4. An HDR environment lighting map ![][image79] (e.g., ![][image80] resolution) is instantiated with uniform energy4.  
During each training step, tile-based rasterization projects material attributes into screen-space G-Buffers: Albedo ![][image81], Normal ![][image82], Roughness ![][image83], Metallic ![][image84], and Depth ![][image85]4. A deferred CUDA/HLSL compute kernel evaluates Cook-Torrance shading per pixel using ![][image79] modulated by cached occlusion maps or ray-traced shadows4.  
The system updates material attributes and ![][image79] weights by backpropagating a composite loss function4:  
![][image86]  
where ![][image87] enforces RGB fidelity (![][image88]), ![][image89] applies Total Variation regularization to penalize high-frequency noise in albedo maps, and ![][image90] drives metallic values toward binary states (![][image91] for dielectrics, ![][image92] for conductors)2.

### **Stage 4: Interactive Relighting Engine Execution**

After factorization converges, the program detaches the optimized environment map ![][image79]4. Users can load custom HDR environment maps or manipulate dynamic point/directional lights4.  
At runtime, the engine rasterizes intrinsic material G-Buffers from target camera view poses4. The image-space deferred shader evaluates Cook-Torrance microfacet equations against the new light sources, generating photorealistic scenes with realistic specularities and dynamic shadows in real time4.

## **Comparative Analysis of Inverse Rendering Frameworks**

The following table summarizes performance, structural characteristics, and technical tradeoffs across primary Gaussian Splatting inverse rendering frameworks:

| Metric / Feature | GS-IR | GaussianShader | 2DGS / IRGS++ | GS-ID | RTR-GS |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Primary Primitive Type** | 3D Gaussian Ellipsoids4 | 3D Gaussian Ellipsoids9 | 2D Planar Surfels10 | 3D Gaussian Ellipsoids5 | 3D Gaussian Ellipsoids3 |
| **Normal Field Formulation** | Linear depth derivation gradient4 | Shortest principal axis alignment7 | Intrinsic surfel normal (![][image93]) \+ ![][image72] \[cite: 11, 13\] | Diffusion-guided normal priors5 | Depth derivation \+ reflection map constraints3 |
| **Material Parameterization** | Albedo, Metallic, Roughness4 | Simplified shading function / BRDF7 | Full Cook-Torrance SVBRDF10 | Albedo, Metallic, Roughness, Specular5 | Albedo, Specular Reflection Map, Deferred BRDF3 |
| **Lighting Parameterization** | Equirectangular HDR Env Map4 | Differentiable HDR Env Map9 | HDR Env Map \+ Ray Sampling10 | Adaptive Spherical Gaussian Mixtures5 | Radiance Transfer \+ HDR Env Map3 |
| **Shadow / Occlusion Mechanism** | Baked SH Occlusion Volumes (![][image59])4 | Approximate environment shading9 | On-the-fly 2D Gaussian Ray Tracing10 | SGM shadow-aware vectors5 | Baked Voxel Visibility \+ Indirect Terms3 |
| **Indirect Light Handling** | SH Illumination Volumes (![][image64])4 | Simplified ambient term9 | Multi-bounce OptiX ray tracing10 | SGM distance decay5 | Radiance transfer rendering branch3 |
| **Runtime Performance** | **![][image94]** (Deferred PBR)4 | ![][image95] (Real-time)9 | ![][image96] (Ray tracing bound)10 | Real-time deferred G-Buffer5 | Real-time deferred branch3 |
| **Primary Advantage** | Compact volumetric caching; high FPS4 | Fast execution; effective glossy highlights7 | Geometrically accurate; rigorous light transport10 | Clean handling of localized light sources5 | Prevents specular highlight albedo baking3 |
| **Primary Drawback** | SH limited to low-frequency shadows4 | Struggles with secondary inter-object shadows12 | Increased VRAM overhead and training duration10 | Complex multi-stage optimization setup5 | Deferred branch increases GPU memory usage3 |

## **Implementation Recommendations for Custom Program Development**

Developing a software program to factorize 3D Gaussian Splats requires choosing primitive representations and visibility mechanisms based on target runtime constraints3.

### **Primitive Selection: 3D Ellipsoids versus 2D Surfels**

3D Gaussian ellipsoids offer high rasterization throughput and fast training convergence1. However, extracting consistent surface normals requires surface-flattening losses, which can introduce noisy geometric artifacts or over-smoothed details6.  
In contrast, 2D Gaussian surfels provide mathematically exact, view-consistent surface normals and ray-splat intersection points2. This geometric definition simplifies normal estimation and enables ray-tracing integration, making 2D surfels the preferred primitive choice for physical inverse rendering10.

### **Visibility Modeling: Volumetric Caching versus Differentiable Ray Tracing**

Volumetric baking (e.g., GS-IR) decouples rendering speed from scene geometric complexity by caching occlusion into low-degree Spherical Harmonics spatial grids4. This yields high frame rates (![][image94]) during relighting4. However, because Spherical Harmonics smooth out directional variation, voxel caching cannot resolve sharp cast shadows from directional light sources4.  
Differentiable ray tracing (e.g., IRGS++) traces explicit shadow rays through a GPU BVH, producing crisp self-shadowing and secondary interreflections10. However, BVH updates and ray traversal increase memory consumption and training duration10.

### **Architectural Recommendation**

For a balanced relighting application that achieves both high visual quality and real-time interactive rendering, the following software architecture is recommended:

> 1. **Primitive Core**: Use 2D Gaussian Surfels as the underlying geometry model, ensuring accurate surface normal calculation without requiring extra depth regularization MLPs11.  
> 2. **Material Pipeline**: Attach explicit Cook-Torrance BRDF properties (![][image97]) directly to surfels and rasterize them into deferred screen-space G-Buffers4.  
> 3. **Hybrid Illumination Engine**: For interactive real-time previewing, evaluate PBR shading in image space using screen-space directional shadow maps and ambient occlusion volumes4. For high-fidelity production rendering, enable an OptiX-accelerated 2D surfel ray-tracing pass to compute precise soft shadows and multi-bounce interreflections10.

By separating primitive geometry, material properties, and environmental illumination into distinct parameters, this architecture enables custom light placement, material editing, and photorealistic asset integration within reconstructed 3D environments4.
